title: CAP Theorem Check
description: Predict which guarantee a system sacrifices and classify CP/AP/CA scenarios.

questions.prompt: According to the CAP theorem, what can a distributed system guarantee during a network partition?

options.text: All three of Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance at once
At most two of Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance
Only Availability, never Consistency
CAP only applies to single-node databases

questions.explanation: CAP theorem: when a partition occurs, a system can only keep two of the three guarantees — typically Consistency+Partition tolerance (CP) or Availability+Partition tolerance (AP).

questions.prompt: A payments ledger rejects/blocks some requests during a network split so that no user ever sees a stale balance. Which guarantee is sacrificed?

options.text: Consistency
Availability
Partition tolerance
Nothing — it keeps all three

questions.explanation: This is a CP system: it keeps Consistency and Partition tolerance, giving up Availability (some requests fail or time out) during a split.

questions.prompt: A social media feed keeps responding during a network split, but some viewers may see slightly stale posts. Which pair does this describe?

options.text: CP — favors consistency
AP — favors availability
CA — no partitions assumed
None of the three; CAP does not apply to feeds

questions.explanation: Always responding (availability) while accepting possibly-stale reads (sacrificing consistency) during a partition is the AP trade-off.

questions.prompt: Why is claiming a distributed system is "CA" usually a red flag in an interview answer?

options.text: CA systems are always faster than CP or AP systems
CA assumes network partitions never happen, which is unrealistic for real distributed systems
CA is not a real combination described by CAP theorem
CA only applies to NoSQL databases

questions.explanation: In practice, partitions will happen. Claiming "CA" without justifying why partitions are impossible (e.g., a true single machine) signals the trade-off wasn't actually considered.

questions.prompt: What is the more interview-effective move when discussing a CAP trade-off: naming the two guarantees you keep, or naming the one you sacrifice?

options.text: Naming the two you keep — it sounds more positive
Naming the one you sacrifice, with a reason tied to the business risk
Neither matters — just say "CAP theorem" and move on
Avoid naming any guarantee and only discuss latency

questions.explanation: Naming the sacrificed guarantee and justifying it (e.g., "a stale balance is worse than a slow response here") demonstrates you understand the real cost of the choice.

questions.prompt: A live sports score ticker must never go down, even if some viewers briefly see an outdated score. Which guarantee is sacrificed?

options.text: Availability
Consistency
Partition tolerance
Scalability

questions.explanation: Staying up (availability) while tolerating stale scores (sacrificing consistency) during a partition is the AP trade-off — consistency is what's given up.
